translations.text: This is the life of the blessed John, the perfect monk, for whom his parents prepared a golden Gospel book.
He completed his good life in perfection and noble endurance on the fourth day of the month of Meshir, in peace. May God bless us all. Amen.
For this life that I am now going to tell you about concerns a man of God, a man worthy of admiration, who lived in our time.
Now there was a man living in the city of Rome who was very rich.
He was the governor of the city.
His name was Eutropius.
His wife's name was Theodora, and both of them had worshiped God since their childhood.
They had three sons.
They secured high positions for two of them in the palace of the emperors.
The youngest, however, they sent to be instructed in the things of God.
After this, he learned the readings of the scholars, and he was among them.
He was also instructed in the things of God and was devoted to the church, seeking God day and night.
One day, a brother who was a monk from the monastery in the interior passed by him.
This monastery is called the Monastery of the Sleepless Ones. He wished to go to Jerusalem to pray in the holy places.
He spoke with John near his house about the word of God.

John was filled with great admiration as he looked at the brother, the monk, and his monastic clothing, and heard his gentle way of speaking and his thoughts, which were directed toward God like fire.
John said, “My lord and father, where are you from? Or your monastery [?]—or where is your monastery?”
The brother, the monk, said to him, “I live in the Monastery of the Sleepless Ones.
And if God wills, I wish to go to Jerusalem and pray there in the holy place. Then, by God's will, I will return to my own place again.”
And the monk told him about everything that John had spoken to him about.
When John heard these words, he took the brother, the monk, by the hand and led him to a quiet place.
He bound him by solemn oaths, saying to him, “My beloved brother, when you go to Jerusalem and return in peace, do not hide yourself from me.
And do not go to your monastery and leave me behind, for I am hiding nothing about my whole life from you. My parents love me very much, more than my brothers.
Indeed, they entrusted me to scholars.
And my father says, ‘I will give you high positions.’
So, according to what he had in mind, he wanted to give me seven other ranks higher than his own.
And after that, he wanted to have me married.
But I too went to church again. I heard them reading a passage that said, “All the glory of this world is a laughing matter.”
And, “Whoever despises this world and follows Christ with an upright heart will scarcely be saved.”
All the more so, my brother, a sinful person like me.
For this reason I beg you, my holy father, to take me with you to your monastery.
When the brother who was a monk heard this, he swore an oath: “When I return, I will take you with me to my monastery.”
Then they immediately confirmed their agreement with one another, and each went to his own dwelling in peace.

After this, the blessed John considered the matter in his heart, saying, “First, let me go to my parents and have them prepare a Gospel book for me to read, because I do not know Christ’s commandments.
And I will also find it in the place where I am going.”
He went to his parents’ house.
He told them a pretext of this sort, saying, “Look, my parents,
I am in [?] among my fellow students, because they are all at school with a golden Gospel book in each one’s possession, which their parents have prepared for them to read.
But I am like a poor person among them who has neither father nor mother.”
John fell on his face at his parents’ feet, saying, “I beg you most earnestly, my parents, prepare a Gospel book for me too, so that I may have it in my hands and learn from it.”
When his mother heard this, she was very glad, because she wanted him to be well educated.
While she was still attending to these things, she spoke to her husband, saying, “My lord and brother, have a golden Gospel book made for our son John.
Do not merely have it written, but also have it beautifully decorated with genuine stones of great value.”
At that very moment his father gave the order.
He brought five hundred gold coins and precious genuine stones and gave them to a master goldsmith.
He made the decoration for a Gospel book that had been written.
His father took it and gave it to his son John.
John took it and rejoiced over it.
And he would study it with great anguish of heart.
And he kept waiting for the brother who was a monk to come, so that he could go with him.
After a few days, the monk came because of the arrangement they had made with each other.
When John saw the monk, he was very happy and rejoiced. He greeted him with great joy.
He said to him, “My lord and father, I know my parents’ wishes and their love for me.
Especially my mother—if she hears of something like this concerning me, her tears will cause me even greater distress.
But I beg you, let us find a way to leave secretly.
And do not let anyone find out about our undertaking.”
The monk said to him, “I will do as you please.
And the Lord will fulfill what you have longed for.”
Then John got up with the monk.
They went away secretly.
They came to the sea, looking for a ship to board.
John spoke to the ship’s captain, saying, “I ask you, my brother, to negotiate your fare with us, so that you will take both of us to the monastery of those who do not sleep.”
The ship’s captain said to them, “Sit here until I have loaded my ship with cargo, and we will sail, God willing.”
John said to the captain, “Tell me how much your fare is.”
The captain said to him, “The fare for my ship is a hundred gold coins.”
Then John said to him, “I will give them to you.”
After John had said these things to the captain, he went to where the monk was.
He said to him, “My father, the ship’s fare is high, and you must see to it that we leave quickly,
so that they do not come upon us, recognize us, and seize us, and we are put to shame because we ran away secretly.”
Then John went into his house to his mother.
He said to her, “I beg you, my dear mother. I know that you have fulfilled all my wishes.
There is just one more thing I lack, which would be an honor for both of us.”
She said to him, “Whatever you want, my son, ask me for it, and I will fulfill it for you.”
John said to his mother, “You know that all the children who are with me at school have invited me not just once,
nor twice, to dine at their homes, eating from what they have.”
I myself had nothing with which to repay them for what they had done for me.
And because of this, shame would not let me go to school again.
His mother said to him, “I will do whatever you want for you.
When your father comes home at noon, I will have him give it to you, so that you can do whatever you want with it together with your friends.”
Then, when his father came home at noon, she told him everything John had said to her.
He answered, “I will give him everything he wants.
But let us assign him a servant to watch over him, because he is a young boy, so that he does not squander it on bad things.”
This proposal pleased them. They called their son John and gave him the gold.
And they assigned the servant to him.
When John received the gold, he went to the place where the monk was, together with the servant accompanying him. He said to him, “My lord and brother, this servant you see belongs to me.
Please let him stay with you while I go to my friends’ place and find out through him when they are coming to see me.”
Then the old monk understood that he was speaking to him about the ship’s sailor.
But he wanted to divert his attention because of the servant accompanying him.
John took the hundred gold coins and went to the ship’s chief sailor.
He said to him, “I beg you, my lord and brother, to get the ship ready so that my brother and I can leave quickly.”
When the sailor heard this—that he wanted to leave secretly—the sailor said to him, “I have already prepared my ship, and I have already told you before that the fare on my ship is high.
But if you stay here until I load my cargo onto the ship, I will take you aboard.”
John said, “I have already told you that I will pay you the fare you named.”
Immediately he brought out the hundred gold coins he had with him, rejoicing greatly.
He gave them to him, saying, “Whatever you told me to pay beyond this, I will give you.
Now see whether the wind [?] for you. Do this for us for God’s sake: get the ship ready quickly so that we can leave secretly.”
When the ship’s sailor heard this, he took the hundred gold coins from him, rejoicing greatly.
He said to John, “Go, get your companion, and come back.
If it is God’s will, I will take good care of you.”
John went back.
He told the brother, the monk, everything that had happened to him.
After another two days, John said to the monk, “Get up, and let us go to the sea, because this is the day when I am to prepare a meal for my friends.
For I want to look for a little fish for them.”
They came to the sea by God’s will.
A favorable wind arose.
The boat’s sailor came and stood a little way off to this side of the boat.
He sat down and beckoned to John and the other monk, saying, “Get up! Come aboard!”
For they were anxious and wanted to separate themselves from the servant and leave him behind,
but they had found no opportunity.
John said to the servant who was accompanying him, “Get up and go to the palace, where the lawyers are, and see whether they have all gathered. Then come and tell me quickly.
Look, I am waiting for you.”
So the servant went away.
They themselves immediately went aboard and cast off the boat.
They came to the monastery by God’s will.
When the servant returned to the sea, he did not find them.
He was deeply troubled in his heart, saying, “Should I run away without telling my master?”
Then he said again, “I am afraid they might search for me, find me, and do me great harm.
Instead, I will go and tell my masters. Perhaps they will take over the search for him from me.
Then I will be free and have nothing to worry about.”
When his mother heard these things, she tore her clothes.
And she put dust on her head.
She wept bitterly, saying, “Woe to me, my beloved son John!
What has happened to you, my sweet son? Woe to me, my son, for they have been jealous of you, O John, my beloved son!
Woe to me!
Who has taken my lamp away from me?
I do not know.”
Woe to me!
Who has taken away my beloved son, the darling of my soul?
O John, my beloved son!
O light of my eyes!
I sent you to gain wisdom; I did not expect the fate that has befallen you.
Woe to me, my son, who is dear to everyone!
Woe to me, my dear son, my beautiful one, whose face is full of every joy!
Woe to me, my image of the angels!
Woe to me! Oh, what will I do from this day on?
Likewise, his other father also wept with sighing and anguish of heart, crying out and saying, “What has happened to you, my beloved son?
I do not know what has happened to you so suddenly.”
When the seven days of mourning were over, during which the whole city mourned with them,
his father then got up, went into the palace, and told the king everything that had happened.
He begged him to send out a decree throughout his kingdom so that people would search for him and perhaps find him.
When the king heard these things, he was deeply grieved and distressed, because he loved him very much for his wisdom
and his knowledge, and because he used to eat with him at his table, owing to his great affection for him.
Then the king sent out an order to soldiers everywhere to search for him. They went around everywhere but did not find him, and they returned to the palace.
When his parents had worn themselves out searching for him without finding him, they gave glory to God.
Meanwhile, John arrived at the monastery with the other monk who was traveling with him.
He brought with him the golden Gospel book that his parents had prepared for him.
He told the superior everything that had happened to the young boy John, and about his great faith in God.
The archimandrite said to the young boy, “My son, I see that you are young in age and very wise in your conduct.
Now, my son, everyone your age who wishes to renounce this world spends forty days persevering. Afterward, they shave the hair from their heads and put the monastic habit on them.”
John said to him, “I implore you, my holy father, by the holy Trinity of one essence and by the prayers of the monastery, to shave my head today.
For God knows that my heart aches for the monastic life and the angelic habit.”
The archimandrite immediately agreed to pray over him, and he clothed him in the angelic habit.
His heart was filled with great joy, and he pleaded with God day and night with great exertion, so that his prayers and his way of life
and his ascetic practices far surpassed those of many around him.
For he had spent six years persevering in this way and in the fear of God.
Indeed, he undertook great acts of discipline and many ascetic practices.
When the archimandrite saw him, he was greatly amazed.
The archimandrite said to him, “My son, you are a young child,
yet here I see you undertaking many great ascetic practices, putting your own body to death, so that you cannot stand up for prayer and fasting.
For excessive self-denial makes a person all the weaker.”
But John did not give up the practices he was undertaking.
When the devil, who hates what is good, saw him, he became intensely angry. He could not bear to see the great acts of discipline, the ascetic practices, and the great honor.
Instead, he brought the memory of his parents into his mind.
Then he kept troubling him about this matter. Along with his frequent fasts and the night vigils that he persistently kept,
his body grew weak, and he wasted away.
When the archimandrite saw him, he was amazed at the weakness that had come over him, so that he was approaching death.
The archimandrite said to him, “Did I not tell you from the beginning that God does not ask anything of us beyond our strength?
But you have grown weak through this great exertion.”
John said to him, “Forgive me, my lord and father. It is not ascetic practice that has made me weak,
but the memory of my parents, which Satan has cast into my heart, and the [?] in my home.
There is also this other matter that you do not know about.
“If he keeps troubling me, I will go to them.
And I trust in God and in your holy prayers that I will trample on all his power and will not violate what is between me and God.
I also know that God will put him to shame.”
The archimandrite said to him, “Did I not tell you that the devil has many tricks? But great is the crown of your perseverance.”
Then the elderly archimandrite wept over the blessed John, because he might turn away from his perseverance.
The next day, John got up and came to the archimandrite.
He threw himself at his feet and wept, saying, “My lord and father, I want to see my parents.”
But I beg you not to stop praying steadfastly for my lowly self,
so that God may perfect me in endurance until I trample on all the enemy’s power. Now give me permission to leave.
The archimandrite had all the brothers gather together to offer fervent prayers for him with many tears.
Then he sent him on his way, saying to him, “My son, go in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
For he is the one who will walk with you, and he is the one who will guide you.”
John got up and took the gold Gospel book that his parents had prepared for him.
He begged the rest of the elders to pray for him.
All of them together stretched out their hands over John’s head, saying, “The prayers of the saints will go with you, so that you may trample on all the enemy’s power.”
At that very moment John got up and greeted all the brothers, saying, “Pray for me, my fathers and brothers.
I greet you all, you blessed people who welcomed me among you and nurtured me with your holy teachings.
I am unworthy of you.”
After receiving the brothers’ farewell greeting, he left the monastery and went away.
When he was a little way outside the monastery, he turned his face back.
He looked at the monastery.
He wept bitterly and profusely.
Then, after weeping, he walked onward until he drew near the city.
While he was still walking, he met a frail man wearing clothes and rags, along with a torn cloak.
He said to him, “Greetings, my brother.
Come and walk with me.”
The brother said to him, “Sir, greetings, my brother.
I too was glad when I saw you. Let us walk together.”
John said to him, “My brother, I see that you are suffering greatly with these clothes and rags you are wearing.
So I beg you to give them to me, and I will give you what I am wearing.”
Immediately John stripped off the clothes he was wearing and gave them to the frail man.
And the frail man blessed John, John.
And they walked together until they reached the city, with the frail man going into it.
Immediately they greeted one another, and each went his own way.
John reached his parents’ city.
He fell down on his face and wept.
He worshiped the Lord, saying, “My Lord Jesus Christ, do not abandon me.”
Then he immediately entered his parents’ gateway. At the door of the house he fell down.
He worshiped the Lord, saying, “Lord Jesus Christ, here is my parents’ house. I have seen it. Give me strength until I trample on all the power of the enemy.”
Immediately John sat down at the entrance to the gateway of his parents’ house.
He slept until morning.
The next day the gatekeeper opened the gate as usual.
He saw John sitting at the entrance, wearing ragged clothes.
He said to him, “What is the matter with you, man? You have dared to come in here
and sit down wearing these shabby clothes!
Get up, move over to this side, and sit down, so I can tidy up my place before my master comes downstairs. Otherwise,
if he sees you, he will quarrel with me.”
John said to him, “I beg you, my brother, do not throw me out, for I am a weak and miserable man.”
The gatekeeper took pity on him.
He let him sit inside his parents’ gateway.
His parents came out in the morning.
John saw them.
He wept so much that his body was soaked with his tears.
But John rejoiced inwardly, saying to himself, “Here are my parents!
you have let me see them.
Now again I believe that you will make me trample on all the power of the enemy.”
Then John immediately wept many more tears, saying,
“My Lord Jesus Christ, do not abandon me.”
He stayed in his parents’ gateway for a whole year.
His father sent him his daily food from his own table, but he did not know that he was his son.
His father would say, “As the Lord lives, my heart aches for this weak man, because he lives among these flies, naked like this, without any clothing on him, day or night.”
John remained in that place and did not want to leave it.
His father would say, “The Lord is merciful, and he will have mercy on us because of him.”
He put a little clothing on him for God's sake, for he was naked night and day. Then one day,
his mother came downstairs.
She saw him in the wretched condition in which he was living, and the [?] of his body.
She felt sick and turned away because of the stench of his body.
His body had wasted away and shriveled from the severe hardship caused by the ascetic practices he was undertaking and the anguish in his heart.
He was like a dead man.
She said to her servants, “Throw this man out of here, because I will not go upstairs.
Unless you throw him out of here, I cannot pass by the place where he is.”
Immediately the servants threw him out of the place where he was.
He got up from that place.
He dragged himself a little farther away.
He did not yet go away and leave the place, but stayed close to the gateway.
When the gatekeeper saw him, he argued with him, saying, “Move away from here, man, because of my mistress, so that she does not see you. She was threatening me because of you.”
But John said to him, “I beg you, my brother, do not undo the kindness you have shown me up to today.
Instead, make me a little hut and a little space where I can go inside, on account of your mistress, so that she will not quarrel with you.”
The gatekeeper did not neglect the matter, but made him the little hut, and he stayed in it. His father sent him his daily provisions from his own table.
But John gave what was sent to him each day as charity to the poor and needy. He ate none of it except bread and salt.
The lame brothers in the city would come to him, and he would feed them.
Because of the intensity of John's ascetic practices, his body became so weak that every one of his bones showed.
After ten full years, when the good God saw his great endurance and his ascetic practices,
and his perseverance, the Lord appeared to him at night in a vision and said to him, “Greetings, John!”
Since you were given the name John, you too have become a virgin like him. Above all, you have left this world behind, with all its glory, and have come and followed me.
Look, the time of the sufferings you have endured and the ascetic practices you have undertaken for my name has come to an end.
I have given you three more days in this world, until you come up to heaven to be with me and rest with my saints.
Then John awoke from the vision.
He wept, saying, “I bless you, my Lord Jesus Christ.
Am I, who am unworthy even to exist, worthy to see the faces of the saints?
But I beg you, my Lord, on behalf of my parents: have mercy on them and forgive their sins, for you alone are sinless, the Lord God, the Almighty alone.”
When the blessed John had said these things, he called Pemnoute.
He said to him, “I know that you have shown me kindness.
Now I want to ask you one more thing: go and tell your mistress this short message that I am going to give you.”
Pemnoute said to him, “Tell me whatever you want, and I will tell her.”
John said to him, “Go and tell her, ‘This poor, weak man outside the gate, whom you ordered to be thrown out, says:
I beg you, my lady, even if you despise me because I am a weak man, do this for me for God’s sake: be so kind as to come here to me, because I have something to tell you.’”
Pemnoute went inside and told her everything John had said to him.
Then she said to him, “What does this beggar want to tell me?
I cannot bear to see him at all, or even to look at him.”
She went inside and told her husband and the members of her household what John had said to Pemnoute.
Her husband said to her, “Go to him, my sister, and find out what he has to tell you.
And do not despise him, for he too is a human being like us.
For it is the weak of the world whom God has chosen.”
But she did not want to go to him.
Again he sent word to her a second time, saying, “I am telling you that I have only three more days in this world.
If you [?], let me speak with you and tell you this before I die.
Otherwise, you will regret it when I die.”
When she heard about his death, she got up and came downstairs.
She said to her servants, “Go and bring him here to me.”
Then the servants called him to her. His mother did not recognize him because of the many ascetic practices he followed.
John, her son, said to her, “[?] The good things you do rise up to God,
as it is written: ‘Whatever you do for someone, you do for me.’ Now,
I am a frail, poor man, and I have nothing with which to repay you for what you and my lord, the ruler, have done for me, or for you to remember me by after my death.
But get up and swear to me that you will do what I tell you
and will not go back on it.
And I will give you what the Lord has appointed for me.”
She said to him, “As the Lord lives, I will do just as you tell me.”
But he said to her, “Swear to me first.”
So she swore to him.
He said to her, “I charge you by the living God: if I die, do not strip me of the clothing I am wearing. Instead, just as I am
now, bury me in it inside this little hut.”
When John had said these things, he brought out the golden Gospel book.
He gave it to her—the one that had been made for him before he became a monk—saying to her, “Let this be a remembrance for you in this age and the age to come.”
She kept turning it this way and that, saying, “This Gospel book looks like the Gospel book that my lord and brother made for my beloved son John.”
Then she remembered and wept bitterly, and her heart became deeply troubled.
She immediately went inside.
She showed it to her husband, saying, “Does this belong to you?”
and see whose it is.”
He recognized it immediately and said, “Truly, this is the Gospel book of our beloved son John. It is none other than his.
Where did this frail man find this? Oh, surely
this man knows where our beloved son John is.”
Then the two of them went out, trembling.
They came to the place where their son lay.
They said to him, “We charge you by the holy, unchanging Trinity and by the great distress that surrounds you: tell us the truth. Where did you find this Gospel book?”
For their hearts were troubled, and their tears were pouring onto the ground.
They could not get up because of their many tears.
He said to them, “Do you not recognize who I am?”
They said to him, “How could we recognize you?”
He said to them, “I am John, your son, and this golden Gospel book is the one I asked you for.
I took it with me to the place where I was going.
But since I longed for the Lord, I clothed myself in his holy power in this humble garb.”
When his parents heard this, they were deeply shaken. They could not hold back their urge to weep, but wept bitterly.
Then they fell upon his chest and embraced him for a long time, from the first watch of the night
until the sixth hour, so that all the palace officials came and wept with them, because they had found John in such great humility.
While his parents were bent over him, the blessed John immediately opened his mouth and gave his spirit into God’s hands.
Oh, how great was the sorrow throughout the whole city that day!
Indeed, loud cries arose among the city’s leading people, the rich and the poor, men and women, young and old.
They all came, wanting to see the blessed John.
His mother, overwhelmed by her suffering and the commotion of the crowds, forgot the oath she had sworn to her son.
Then she had him stripped of the ragged clothes he was wearing and the other coarse garments, and she dressed him in an honored robe worthy of royalty.
Immediately an angel came
and touched his mother’s feet.
They knocked against each other with trembling and severe spasms because of the oath to her son John that she had forgotten.
Then his father came and saw her in torment. He said to her, “Truly, my sister, this has happened to you because of the oath to our son John that you disregarded.”
Then this matter troubled them.
They removed the fine clothes from him
and put the ragged clothes back on him as before.
Immediately the spasms in her feet stopped.
She raised her voice and wept in great anguish, saying, “Woe to me, my beloved son John!”
Oh, what has happened to you, the light of my eyes, that you have come down to such great humiliation and such great poverty!
Blessed is my bosom, for it carried you, and my breasts, for they nourished you, O my holy son!
The whole crowd marveled at the young boy’s virtue, at how he had controlled himself with such endurance, and they gave glory to God.
His parents buried him in the hut, as he had told them, and built a shrine over him.
They took everything they owned.
They distributed it to the poor and needy.
Afterward his parents ended their lives well, giving glory to God, with the prayers of our holy fathers.
This is the struggle of Saint John, in which he proved strong, for he girded himself.
He served the Lord Jesus Christ with great endurance, so that he might obtain favor for us before God and forgive us our many sins.
Through him, glory be to him and his good Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.
Written on Mechir 23, in the first indiction, in the year [?] of the holy martyrs, year 363.
I, the wretched sinner Victor, the least of deacons, son of the blessed Mercurius, deacon, son of the blessed Eponychus, archdeacon,
of Saint Mercurius, the great commander, from Latopolis, wrote this book. Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom. 99.
Through the zeal and care of our God-loving brother [?], Zechariah, the deacon and monk of Saint Mercurius on the mountain of Tbo,
he prepared this book through his own labor and donated it to the monastery of Saint Mercurius on the mountain of Tbo,
where he lives, for the salvation of his soul, so that Saint Mercurius and all the other saints whose commemorations we have written in this book, each by name,
may bless him with every spiritual and heavenly blessing, and grant him endurance and save him from all the snares of the devil and of wicked people,
and enable him to fulfill the service of the holy place and the calling allotted to him, namely that of deacon and monk.
When he completes the course of this life, according to what is appointed for everyone,
may Saint Mercurius and the other saints whose names are written in this book intercede with Christ on his behalf,
and may he place him in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and may he receive an inheritance with the fathers of the community, Apa Palamon and Pachomius,
and Horsiesius, and Apa Petronius, and Theodore, and Apa Shenoute, and all the saints, and may he be worthy to hear:
“Well done, good and faithful servant! Since you were trustworthy in small matters, I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.”
Amen. So be it. 99.
